chunks.text: 2 Results Because our method yields a continuous decision variable, we can freely choose the operating point on the ROC curve by setting the classification threshold, enabling task- and use-case-specific trade-offs between sensitivity and specificity. In the following, we first report threshold-independent discrimination (AUROC) and then analyze how threshold selection affects clinically relevant operating characteristics. 2.1 Overall performance (AUROC) First, we compared the binary classification ability of the three approaches, independent of a set threshold, using the AUROC. Table 1 shows the average AUROC across all classes for the different datasets using MedGemma-27B. All reported metrics stem from the independent test set, with decision thresholds derived solely from the validation split. The values for the individual CheXpert classes are visualized in Figure 3 and are provided in the supplementary material. To assess statistical significance, we calculated pairwise differences and corresponding two-sided p p -values (Table 2 ). The normalization approach demonstrated a statistically significant improvement in mean AUROC for five of the six datasets compared to text-elicited probability estimates. Similarly, compared to using raw token probabilities, normalization provided a statistically significant advantage on three of the six datasets. For the MIMIC and NCT-CRC-HE datasets, however, raw token probabilities yielded a small but statistically significant advantage. For the G1020 dataset, no approach was significantly better than the others. Figure 3 : Class-specific AUROC values for the CheXpert dataset using MedGemma-27B. The three bars for each class represent normalized token probabilities, raw token probabilities (“Unnormalized” in the legend), and text-elicited probability estimates (“Text”). Error bars indicate 95% confidence intervals. The “average” bars show the mean across classes.

2.2 Effect of the decision threshold The AUROC provides a threshold-independent measure of class separability. However, practical classification requires defining a specific decision threshold. We examined the threshold implicitly set by the LLM’s default behavior of sampling the most likely token, which corresponds to a threshold of 0.5 in our normalized probability scheme. Figure 4 illustrates how the choice of operating point determines the clinically relevant balance between sensitivity and specificity. It shows the ROC curves for several example classes, comparing the default threshold (0.5) with an “optimal” threshold that maximizes the sum of sensitivity and specificity (selected on the validation set). For the “No Finding” class on the CheXpert dataset (Fig. 4(a) ), MedGemma-27B achieves a high AUROC of 0.921, indicating strong class separability. However, at the default threshold the model effectively labels all studies as abnormal (i.e., answers no to “No Finding”), yielding a sensitivity of 0.0 and a specificity of 1.0—an operating point that is clinically unhelpful because it fails to identify any radiographically normal examinations. By shifting the threshold using the validation set to 0.005, the sensitivity increased to 0.945 while yielding a specificity of 0.696. Conversely, for the “Support Devices” class (Fig. 4(c) ), the default threshold yielded a very high sensitivity of 0.994 but a poor specificity of 0.108. Adjusting the threshold to 0.899 resulted in a sensitivity of 0.740 and a specificity of 0.819. For “Pleural Effusion” (Fig. 4(b) ), the implicit threshold is closer to the optimal point, but adjustment still offers improvement, moving from a sensitivity of 0.700 and specificity of 0.900 to a sensitivity of 0.850 and specificity of 0.792 at a threshold of 0.072. These examples demonstrated that the model’s default operating point is often suboptimal and that the optimal threshold is highly class-dependent.

A comparison between the medically adapted MedGemma models and their general-purpose Gemma-3 counterparts underscored the value of domain-specific fine-tuning (Table 3 ). The performance gap was most pronounced for chest radiography; on CheXpert, for instance, the MedGemma-27B model achieved an average AUROC of 0.819, substantially outperforming the Gemma-3-27B’s score of 0.535. Similar gains were observed on the MIMIC-CXR dataset. For histopathology classification on NCT-CRC-HE, the gain was pronounced for the 4B models (0.817 vs. 0.687) but small for the 27B models (0.783 vs. 0.769). Unexpectedly, however, the general-purpose models outperformed the MedGemma variants on the dermatology datasets (DERM12345 for both model sizes and HAM10000 for the 27B models), despite the latter having been fine-tuned on dermatological images [ 18 ] . Differences between models were not formally tested. 2.3 Distribution of Optimal Thresholds Figure 5 illustrates the deviation of the optimal thresholds from the implicit default threshold of 0.5 across the different CheXpert classes. For 11 of the 13 classes, the optimal threshold lies below the implicit threshold determined by the model’s training. This indicates that for these findings, the model exhibits a bias toward negative classification, resulting in higher specificity than sensitivity at the implicitly set threshold of 0.5. When all findings of an image were queried in a single call, the latency per finding decreased to 12–14 ms; for example, all 14 CheXpert findings of one radiograph were assessed in about 0.2 s. 3 Discussion Our results demonstrate that the implicit classification threshold used by large language models is often suboptimal for binary classification tasks in medicine. By extracting and normalizing the probabilities of yes and no tokens, we can define a continuous score that allows for threshold selection, improving the diagnostic utility of these models.

This simple, post-hoc method reveals that while a model may have strong discriminative capabilities (as measured by AUROC), its default output corresponds to a fixed operating point that is often poorly suited to the clinical task. The comparison of the three approaches in Table 1 shows that normalizing the yes and no token probabilities yields the highest AUROC for MedGemma-27B on four of six datasets, whereas raw probabilities were slightly but significantly better on MIMIC-CXR and NCT-CRC-HE. This suggests that the raw logit values for these two tokens contain the most relevant signal for the binary task, and that the influence of other vocabulary tokens is a source of noise. For MedGemma-27B, the raw-probability approach achieved higher AUROC values than text-elicited probability estimates on all six datasets (not formally tested), but it is still influenced by probability mass assigned to irrelevant vocabulary tokens. The poorer performance of prompting the model to output a probability as text, despite constrained decoding, suggests that these models are not reliably calibrated to express their internal uncertainty as an accurate numeric value. The observation that, for MedGemma-27B, raw token probabilities outperform direct text inference (for the other models, the ordering varied across datasets), which contrasts with the findings of Gu et al. [ 20 ] , may have two potential explanations. First, our evaluation uses different models and focuses exclusively on image-based tasks, whereas their work included text. Second, our use of guided decoding ensures a valid numerical output for every sample. In contrast, the unconstrained generation used by Gu et al. might yield non-numerical responses (e.g., “I don’t know”), which would be excluded from their analysis and could introduce a selection bias.

The class- and dataset-dependent nature of the optimal threshold, as seen in Figure 4 , highlights the necessity of selecting the decision threshold for specific use cases. Figure 5 shows the deviation between the implicit and optimal thresholds across CheXpert classes. For 11 of 13 classes, the optimal threshold falls below 0.5, indicating a pronounced model bias toward negative predictions. This misaligned default threshold has important clinical ramifications, as different applications demand different operating points. For instance, screening tasks require high sensitivity to minimize missed diagnoses, necessitating a lower threshold than confirmatory tests, where high specificity is essential to avoid false positives. These results demonstrate that no universal threshold exists across all classes and datasets; optimal threshold selection must be adapted to the specific clinical context and task requirements. Our approach shares a central idea with recently introduced decision models such as Jev [ 10 ] : rather than generating text, the model is queried once and returns the probability of a predefined answer that downstream software can threshold. Unlike Jev, which is a proprietary, text-only model trained with a dedicated objective for calibrated decisions, our approach requires no additional training, uses open-weight models, and applies to image inputs. Notably, early independent evaluations of Jev found that no single temperature fitted all tasks and recommended selecting the decision threshold on a local selection set and re-checking it on held-out items [ 21 ] . Similarly, a benchmark of Jev on 37 datasets found that its binary probabilities ranked cases well but were poorly placed relative to a fixed threshold of 0.5 [ 22 ] . On four of these datasets, thresholds tuned on training data improved performance both for Jev and for open LLMs whose yes/no probabilities were read out and renormalized as in our study [ 22 ] .

This mirrors our observation that optimal thresholds vary strongly across classes and datasets, suggesting that local threshold selection remains necessary regardless of how the probabilities are produced. In our setting, a single decision took a median of 53–79 ms on one GPU, which is comparable to the latencies reported for such decision models (70–500 ms [ 10 ] ), although these figures are not directly comparable, as the latter include the overhead of a hosted API. The performance of MedGemma varies significantly across tasks. While it shows strong performance on some classes, such as “No Finding” on CheXpert or “Lymphocytes” on NCT-CRC-HE, its performance on other tasks is close to random, indicating the current limitations of generalist medical models. The AUROC analysis is crucial here, as it distinguishes between a poorly placed default threshold (a high AUROC with a suboptimal default threshold) and a genuine inability of the model to perform the task (an AUROC close to 0.5). Future work could explore extending this method to a chain-of-thought setting. One could potentially extract the probabilities from the final yes or no token after a reasoning process. However, the reasoning itself would likely bias the final token probabilities, potentially skewing them heavily and diminishing the utility of the thresholding approach. Investigating this interaction remains an open question. Our method relies on access to the token probabilities (or logits), which may not be available for closed-source models accessed via APIs. While one could theoretically estimate these probabilities by sampling many single-token answers, this would likely be impractical for most applications. Furthermore, this study was limited to binary classification.

Extending this approach to multi-class problems would require further methodological development, for instance, by performing one-vs-rest classification for each class or by normalizing probabilities across a larger set of verbalizer tokens. For NCT-CRC-HE-100K, no mapping of patches to their source slides is publicly available, so validation and test patches may originate from the same slides. This does not affect the AUROC, which is computed on the test set alone, but the metrics at the validation-optimized threshold may be slightly optimistic. Furthermore, classification performance is sensitive to prompt formulation and structure. The model’s true discriminative ability for certain classes may therefore exceed our observed results if suboptimal prompt design limits class separability. In this paper, we have presented a simple yet effective method to improve the binary classification performance of large language models by shifting their decision threshold. We have shown that the default threshold, implicitly defined by greedy token sampling, is often suboptimal for medical applications. By normalizing the probabilities of yes and no answer tokens, we can create a tunable score that allows for the selection of an appropriate operating point on the ROC curve, balancing sensitivity and specificity for the clinical task at hand. This approach enhances the reliability of LLMs in medical diagnostics and provides a framework for evaluating and deploying them more safely and effectively. 4 Methods All experiments were conducted using Python (version 3.12.3) and the vLLM library (version 0.9.2) for model inference. We evaluated four open-access models: the medically fine-tuned multimodal MedGemma 4B and MedGemma 27B [ 18 ] , alongside their architecture-matched general-purpose counterparts Gemma 3 4B and Gemma 3 27B [ 19 ] . All four models are based on the Gemma 3 architecture, with the MedGemma variants further adapted for medical data.

For each classification task, we formulated a prompt that queried the presence of a specific clinical finding (see supplementary material for details), instructing the model to answer with a single token: yes or no . This setup led the model to assign a high probability to one of the two designated verbalizer tokens. The model input X X consisted of the task-specific prompt concatenated with an image. Decoding was constrained to a single token and terminated immediately. From the first-step distribution, we extracted the raw token probabilities p raw ​ ( 𝚢𝚎𝚜 ∣ X ) p_{\text{raw}}(\mathtt{yes}\!\mid\!X) and p raw ​ ( 𝚗𝚘 ∣ X ) p_{\text{raw}}(\mathtt{no}\!\mid\!X) , which are the probabilities assigned by the model to the 𝚢𝚎𝚜 \mathtt{yes} or 𝚗𝚘 \mathtt{no} token given the input X X . To account for any residual probability mass on tokens outside this binary set [ 4 ] , we normalized the probabilities over the two relevant tokens: p norm ​ ( 𝚢𝚎𝚜 ∣ X ) = p raw ​ ( 𝚢𝚎𝚜 ∣ X ) p raw ​ ( 𝚢𝚎𝚜 ∣ X ) + p raw ​ ( 𝚗𝚘 ∣ X ) . p_{\text{norm}}(\mathtt{yes}\!\mid\!X)=\frac{p_{\text{raw}}(\mathtt{yes}\!\mid\!X)}{p_{\text{raw}}(\mathtt{yes}\!\mid\!X)+p_{\text{raw}}(\mathtt{no}\!\mid\!X)}. (1) This is equivalent to a two-class softmax function applied only to the logits of yes and no . The complementary probability, p norm ​ ( 𝚗𝚘 ∣ X ) p_{\text{norm}}(\mathtt{no}\!\mid\!X) , is calculated analogously, and the two probabilities sum to one by construction. Throughout our analysis, we treated p norm ​ ( 𝚢𝚎𝚜 ∣ X ) p_{\text{norm}}(\mathtt{yes}\!\mid\!X) as the predicted probability of the positive class. Since the denominator is shared, p norm ​ ( 𝚢𝚎𝚜 ∣ X ) > 0.5 p_{\text{norm}}(\mathtt{yes}\!\mid\!X)>0.5 if and only if p raw ​ ( 𝚢𝚎𝚜 ∣ X ) > p raw ​ ( 𝚗𝚘 ∣ X ) p_{\text{raw}}(\mathtt{yes}\!\mid\!X)>p_{\text{raw}}(\mathtt{no}\!\mid\!X) . Thus, greedy decoding, for example by setting the temperature to 0 or top-k to 1, is equivalent to applying a fixed classification threshold of 0.5.

We used p norm ​ ( 𝚢𝚎𝚜 ∣ X ) p_{\text{norm}}(\mathtt{yes}\!\mid\!X) as a continuous score to sweep the decision threshold across the interval [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] , which allowed us to generate ROC curves and compute the AUROC as a threshold-independent measure of performance [ 23 ] . For a fixed threshold, we reported accuracy as T ​ P + T ​ N T ​ P + T ​ N + F ​ P + F ​ N \frac{TP+TN}{TP+TN+FP+FN} , sensitivity (true positive rate) as T ​ P T ​ P + F ​ N \frac{TP}{TP+FN} , and specificity (true negative rate) as T ​ N T ​ N + F ​ P \frac{TN}{TN+FP} , where T ​ P TP denotes true positives, T ​ N TN true negatives, F ​ P FP false positives, and F ​ N FN false negatives. In addition to this token-probability-based scoring, we evaluated a complementary method evaluated by Gu et al. [ 20 ] , which involves explicitly prompting the model to output a numerical probability for the presence of a finding as text. To ensure machine-readability and prevent cases where no valid probability could be extracted, we employed a constrained JSON template (see Supplement) that permitted only numeric outputs with three decimal places (all observed values lay between 0 and 1). We also included results using the raw probability, p raw ​ ( 𝚢𝚎𝚜 ∣ X ) p_{\text{raw}}(\mathtt{yes}\!\mid\!X) , directly. To prevent bias from intra-context leakage, we elicited only a single probability within any given context window, as requesting multiple probabilities or classes in the same context could allow the model to condition later outputs on earlier ones. 4.1 Datasets For datasets with more than 10,000 images, we randomly subsampled 10,000 instances to keep the evaluation computationally tractable. We then split this subsample into 5,000 validation instances (used only to select the decision threshold) and 5,000 test instances (used only for the final performance evaluation).

If a dataset provides official validation and test splits, we used those; otherwise, we used all available data and created random validation/test splits as described above. For chest radiography, we evaluated our method on two datasets: CheXpert [ 24 ] and MIMIC-CXR-JPG [ 25 , 26 , 27 ] . From CheXpert, we included the official test set of 668 images, for which the reference standard was established by a majority vote of five board-certified radiologists, alongside 234 validation images. As the label “Fracture” has no positive cases in the validation split, no decision threshold could be derived for it. We therefore included all 14 CheXpert labels in the AUROC analysis but excluded “Fracture” from the threshold analysis, resulting in 13 labels there. From MIMIC-CXR-JPG v2.0.0, we used the official test split, which comprises 3,269 studies (5,159 images), while the validation set consists of 1,808 studies (2,991 images). For studies with multiple images (e.g., frontal and lateral views), all images of the study were provided to the model together. For histopathology, we used NCT-CRC-HE-100K, which provides 100,000 non-overlapping H&E-stained patches ( 224 × 224 224\times 224 pixels at 0.5 ​ μ ​ m / px 0.5\,\mu\mathrm{m/px} ) from nine tissue classes [ 28 ] . We sampled 10,000 patches for our evaluation, which were randomly split into 5,000 test and 5,000 validation images. In ophthalmology, we used the full G1020 dataset, consisting of 1,020 high-resolution fundus images with glaucoma ground truth and pixel-level optic disc/cup annotations [ 29 ] . It was split into 204 test and 816 validation images. For dermatology, we used the HAM10000 dataset in its ISIC Archive version, which provides 11,720 dermatoscopic images with diagnoses verified by histopathology, follow-up, or expert consensus, organized into three hierarchical diagnosis levels with 18 classes in total [ 30 ] .

We sampled 10,000 images, which were randomly split into 5,000 test and 5,000 validation images. Additionally, we used DERM12345, which provides 12,345 dermatoscopic images; we used the first three levels of its hierarchical diagnosis labels, comprising 37 classes [ 31 ] . We sampled 10,000 images, which were also randomly split into 5,000 test and 5,000 validation images. For each dataset, we created binary “yes/no” prompts asking for each class. Of the datasets used, MIMIC was the only one included in the training data for the MedGemma models [ 18 ] . Conversely, the authors of MedGemma stated that the CheXpert dataset was not used at any stage of model development, which makes it an ideal benchmark for external validation. 4.2 Statistical Analysis We estimated 95% confidence intervals (CIs) and two-sided p p -values using nonparametric bootstrap resampling with 10,000 replicates. To adjust for multiple comparisons across 12 tests, we applied a Bonferroni correction, resulting in a per-comparison significance threshold of α = 0.0042 \alpha=0.0042 . 4.3 Inference Latency To quantify the computational cost of our approach, we measured the end-to-end latency of a single decision, i.e., one forward pass that generates a single token and returns the log-probabilities of yes and no , using vLLM on a single NVIDIA H100 GPU. We used the prompts of all six datasets together with randomly sampled images from five datasets, with a new image for every query to prevent reuse of cached image tokens. We report the median latency over 51 single queries per model, as well as the latency per finding when all findings of one image were queried in a single call. 4.4 Ethics This retrospective study used only publicly available, de-identified datasets. Ethical approval and informed consent were therefore not required for this secondary analysis; access to MIMIC-CXR-JPG was obtained through PhysioNet in accordance with its data use agreement.

Conversely, the authors of MedGemma stated that the CheXpert dataset was not used at any stage of model development, which makes it an ideal benchmark for external validation.
